outcome: Since 26 January 2024 one event bears on this problem: Pavelescu, Pavelescu and Potter (arXiv:2604.03433, 3 April 2026) prove that every simple graph of order 13 with minimum degree 6 either contains a K6 minor or is apex and isomorphic to K1 ∗ Ic, which the abstract calls a proof of Jørgensen's conjecture for order 13 and §1 calls a strengthening of it; the general conjecture (every 6-connected K6-minor-free graph is apex) remains open on every source I could reach, and no source names an AI system for it.
problem_asks: (1) A universal claim over all finite simple graphs G, with no bound on the number of vertices. (2) Hypothesis: G is 6-vertex-connected. (3) Hypothesis: G has no K6 minor. (4) Conclusion: G is an apex graph, meaning there is a vertex v of G such that G minus v is planar. The statement does not ask for a specific v, a bound on |V(G)|, or a description of G beyond apexness. It has no parent and no separate sub-claims; the literature states it with the same hypotheses and conclusion (Conjecture 1.1 in Kawarabayashi, Norine, Thomas and Wollan).

events.what_happened: L. K. Jørgensen, 'Contractions to K8', Journal of Graph Theory 18(5):431-448 (1994), where the conjecture is posed. The 2026 preprint (§4) and Odeneal and Pavelescu (2019) both quote it as 'every 6-connected graph which does not have a K6 minor is apex', and the 2026 preprint attributes to this paper the result that every simple graph of order at most 11 with minimum degree at least 6 contains a K6 minor. I did not open the 1994 paper; the statement and that claim come from the citing papers.
events.delivers: Poses the conjecture in the stated form. As reported by citing papers, it also settles the minimum-degree-6 statement for order at most 11; 6-connected graphs of those orders are vacuous cases, since 6-connectivity forces minimum degree at least 6.
events.remains: Every order 12 and above, including all 6-connected K6-minor-free graphs on 12 or more vertices.
events.time_since_posted: about 32 years (1994 to 2026); the statement is quoted in 2019 and 2026 papers, but I found no separate check of the 1994 argument
events.direction: Poses the conjecture. The reported order-11 min-degree-6 result is consistent with it.

events.what_happened: Kawarabayashi, Norine, Thomas and Wollan, 'K6 minors in large 6-connected graphs', arXiv:1203.2192 (v1, 9 March 2012, 47 pages). Abstract: 'Jorgensen conjectured that every 6-connected graph with no K6 minor has a vertex whose deletion makes the graph planar. We prove the conjecture for all sufficiently large graphs.' Theorem 1.3 (ar5iv text): there is an absolute constant N such that every 6-connected graph on at least N vertices with no K6 minor is apex. Journal version: J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 129 (2018) 158-203, DOI 10.1016/j.jctb.2017.09.007, published March 2018 per Crossref. (The Open Problem Garden gives 2019 for this volume; Crossref gives 2018.)
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only (9 Mar 2012). Journal version JCTB 129 (2018) 158-203, published March 2018 per Crossref.
events.delivers: For every 6-connected graph G with at least N vertices and no K6 minor, G is apex. The restriction is size: N is an absolute constant that the abstract does not quantify and that the theorem does not state numerically. No restriction on treewidth, girth or connectivity beyond 6-connectivity.
events.remains: 6-connected K6-minor-free graphs on fewer than N vertices, except that orders 12 and 13 are covered by later events and orders at most 11 are vacuous (6-connectivity forces minimum degree 6, which Jørgensen's order-11 result excludes). Since N is unstated, the remaining range is not quantified.

events.what_happened: Kawarabayashi, Norine, Thomas and Wollan, 'K6 minors in 6-connected graphs of bounded tree-width', arXiv:1203.2171 (v1 9 March 2012; v2 5 April 2013). Theorem 1.2 (ar5iv text): for every w >= 1 there is an N such that every 6-connected graph on at least N vertices with tree-width at most w and no K6 minor is apex. The introduction calls this 'the first step' toward the all-large-graphs statement. Journal version: J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 136 (2019) 1-32, DOI 10.1016/j.jctb.2017.08.006, published May 2019 per Crossref. The text also carries the line '8 April 2005, revised 3 April 2013'; I did not treat that as a public date, since the first public version on arXiv is March 2012.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 (9 Mar 2012) and v2 (5 Apr 2013). Journal version JCTB 136 (2019) 1-32, published May 2019 per Crossref.
events.delivers: For each fixed treewidth bound w, every 6-connected K6-minor-free graph on at least N(w) vertices and of treewidth at most w is apex. Restricted to bounded treewidth; N(w) is not given in the abstract.
events.remains: 6-connected K6-minor-free graphs of unbounded treewidth, and graphs of bounded treewidth below the unstated N(w). The large-graph theorem above covers all sufficiently large graphs, including this class.

events.what_happened: Elad Aigner-Horev and Roi Krakovski, 'Extremal results regarding K6-minors in graphs of girth at least 5', arXiv:1012.5795 (v1, 28 December 2010, 14 KB). Abstract: every 6-connected graph of girth at least 6 contains a K6 minor; and a 6-connected n-vertex graph with at least 16n/5 - 8 edges and girth at least 5 contains a K6 minor. The authors state that the girth-6 result 'settles the Jorgensen conjecture for graphs of girth >= 6'. Published: Journal of Combinatorics 2(3) (2011) 463-479, DOI 10.4310/joc.2011.v2.n3.a7 (Crossref).
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only. The comments field says '13 pages, submitted on October 12 2010', which refers to an earlier submission, not a public version.
events.delivers: Every 6-connected graph of girth at least 6 has a K6 minor, so the class of 6-connected girth-6 K6-minor-free graphs is empty and contains no counterexample. Restricted to girth at least 6.
events.remains: 6-connected K6-minor-free graphs of girth at most 5 (the girth-5 result is a size bound, not a resolution).

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper, vol. 2, no. 3, pp. 463-479 (2011) per Crossref

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture on girth at least 6, where it holds vacuously.

events.what_happened: Ryan Odeneal and Andrei Pavelescu, 'Simple graphs of order 12 and minimum degree 6 contain K6 minors', arXiv:1910.11891 (v1 25 October 2019, 8 KB; v2 27 January 2020, 13 pages, 7 figures). Abstract: 'We prove that every simple graph of order 12 which has minimum degree 6 contains a K6 minor.' The paper quotes Jørgensen's 1994 conjecture and notes the order-12 case is thereby vacuously true; it lists as open whether every simple graph of order at most 14 with minimum degree at least 6 that is not apex contains a K6 minor. Published: Involve 13 (2020) 829-843, DOI 10.2140/involve.2020.13.829, published 5 December 2020 per Crossref.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 25 Oct 2019 (8 KB); v2 27 Jan 2020 (5.3 MB, 13 pages, 7 figures). Journal Involve 13 (2020), published 5 Dec 2020. I did not check whether v1 already contains the full argument.
events.delivers: Every simple graph of order 12 with minimum degree 6 contains a K6 minor, so the conjecture holds at order 12. Restricted to one order and to the minimum-degree-6 hypothesis.
events.remains: Every order other than 12, including order 14 (listed as open in the minimum-degree form) and all orders 13 and above that the other events do not cover.

events.what_happened: Talk abstracts, not a written paper. Robin Thomas, with Sergey Norin (the search snippets call it joint work), announced that for every integer t there is an N_t such that every t-connected graph on at least N_t vertices with no K_t minor has a set of at most t-5 vertices whose deletion leaves it planar, and that t-connectivity and t-5 cannot be lowered. The earliest talk record I found is an IWOCA 2009 abstract (PDF metadata dated May 2009); an IPAM abstract page also exists (its text did not render); a 2010 talk is mentioned in a search snippet. Thomas's slides state the same theorem. At t = 6 this gives a second route to the large-graph apex statement. I found no arXiv or journal write-up of the general theorem.
events.delivers: Per the talk abstracts only: for t = 6, every 6-connected K6-minor-free graph on at least N_6 vertices has a single vertex whose deletion leaves a planar graph (apex), with N_6 not stated. Restricted to large graphs.
events.remains: 6-connected K6-minor-free graphs on fewer than N_6 vertices (N_6 not given).
events.time_since_posted: about 16 years (talk 2009); no written version located
events.doubts: No written proof located. The statement rests on talk abstracts and slides; the PDFs did not decode for me, so the statement comes from search snippets of those pages. Whether the t-5 theorem was ever published, and in what form, is unknown to me.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture for large graphs at t = 6, if the talk claims stand.

events.what_happened: Andrei Pavelescu, Elena Pavelescu and Madeline Potter, 'New minor minimal non-apex graphs', arXiv:2604.03433 (v1, 3 April 2026, 12 pages, 4 figures; no later version). Theorem 1 (§1; restated without 'apex' in §4): a simple graph of order 13 with minimum degree 6 either contains a K6 minor or is apex and isomorphic to K1 ∗ Ic. The abstract says this proves Jørgensen's conjecture for order 13; §1 says it strengthens 'Jørgensen's conjecture that every 6-connected graph of order 13 without a K6 minor is apex'. The paper also lists the minor-minimal non-apex graphs on at most 12 vertices (177 graphs) and at most 26 edges (286), 339 in total with 44 new, per §2 as read through the HTML version; that part concerns apex obstructions, not this problem. The paper describes its findings as computer-assisted: nauty generates graphs, NetworkX is used, a minor-search tool ('minor miner') checks K6 minors, and two programs ran for a combined 340 hours. It reports that all 367,860 six-regular 2-connected graphs of order 13 have a K6 minor.
events.revisions: v1 only (3 Apr 2026) as of 12 Oct 2026.
events.delivers: For graphs of order exactly 13: every simple graph of order 13 with minimum degree 6 contains a K6 minor or is apex and isomorphic to K1 ∗ Ic. Because a 6-connected graph has minimum degree at least 6, this covers every 6-connected K6-minor-free graph of order 13 and needs only the weaker minimum-degree hypothesis. Restricted to a single vertex count; the proof is a finite computation over graphs of order 13, supported by exhaustive enumeration.
events.remains: Every order other than 13. Orders 12 and at most 11 are covered by earlier events; orders 14 up to the unstated N of the large-graph theorem remain open, and order 14 is listed as open in the minimum-degree form.
events.directly_checkable: The order-13 claim is a finite computation over 13-vertex graphs of minimum degree 6, checkable in principle with nauty and a K6-minor test. The paper gives its code as an ancillary file (NewMMNA_code.pdf), which I did not open.
events.doubts: (a) A single-group preprint with no peer review, journal reference, or independent reproduction found. (b) The argument is computer-assisted: exhaustive enumeration, a minor-search program, and about 340 hours of computation; the code is an ancillary file I did not open, so I have not verified the computations. (c) Wording varies within the paper: the abstract and §4 say 'proving' or state the theorem without 'apex' in the conclusion; §1 says 'strengthens'. (d) The hypothesis is minimum degree 6, not 6-connectivity; this is a different statement that implies the 6-connected case at order 13. (e) The full PDF did not decode for me; §1-§4 were read through a summarising fetch of the HTML version, so the quoted wording is not verbatim from a full text. None of these is evidence that the result is wrong.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture: no order-13 counterexample is found, and the one graph exempted from K6-minor containment is apex.
events.object: The graph K1 ∗ Ic: the icosahedron Ic joined to one extra vertex, 13 vertices in total, which the theorem names as the only order-13 minimum-degree-6 graph with no K6 minor. It is apex, since deleting the joined vertex leaves the planar icosahedron. It is an explicit graph, not a non-constructive existence proof. It is not a counterexample to the conjecture, since it is apex. I did not verify that it is 6-connected.

ai.disclosed_cost: Compute, not AI: the paper reports the computations ran on an Apple M4 Pro with 24 GB of memory and 14 cores for a combined 340 hours across two programs (§3, read through the HTML version).

disputes.summary: The large-graph theorem is credited to four authors (Kawarabayashi, Norine, Thomas, Wollan) in the arXiv and JCTB records. The Open Problem Garden entry credits 'DeVos, Hegde, Kawarabayashi, Norine, Thomas, and Wollan', and a talk-abstract listing does the same. A search snippet says the arXiv paper acknowledges DeVos and Hegde as contributors who did not want co-authorship; I did not confirm that in the paper's text. The Open Problem Garden also gives JCTB 2019 for the 2018 volume.

summary: As far as my searches reach, Jørgensen's conjecture (every 6-vertex-connected K6-minor-free graph is apex) is still open in general. The Wikipedia list entry, in the Graph theory section under 'Restriction of graph parameters', reads 'Jørgensen's conjecture that every 6-vertex-connected K6-minor-free graph is an apex graph'; the Apex graph article says it 'remains unproven'. Before the window, five events settle or move parts of it, and a sixth is a talk-level claim: the 1994 origin (Jørgensen, known to me only through citing papers); the large-graph theorem of Kawarabayashi, Norine, Thomas and Wollan (arXiv March 2012, JCTB 2018), with an unstated N; its bounded-treewidth companion (arXiv March 2012, JCTB 2019); Aigner-Horev and Krakovski's girth-6 result (arXiv December 2010, J. Combinatorics 2011); Odeneal and Pavelescu's order-12 result (arXiv October 2019, Involve 2020); and Norin and Thomas's general t-5 deletion theorem, which at t = 6 gives the large-graph apex statement again, known from talk abstracts only, with no write-up located. Inside the window there is one event: Pavelescu, Pavelescu and Potter, arXiv:2604.03433 (3 April 2026), which proves that every order-13 graph with minimum degree 6 has a K6 minor or is apex and isomorphic to K1 ∗ Ic. This is the close call. The abstract says it proves the conjecture for order 13; §1 says it strengthens it; and the argument is a finite, computer-assisted enumeration (nauty, NetworkX, a minor search, about 340 hours), with no proof assistant. Under the scope rule it is either a complete restricted case (one vertex count, with a human-stated argument) or a finite check of one instance-size, which the rule says moves nothing about a universal claim; I record both readings and do not choose. Its hypothesis is minimum degree 6, a weaker assumption than 6-connectivity, so it covers every 6-connected graph of order 13. I found no public engagement with it and no later paper citing it; the arXiv listing shows no journal reference. For AI involvement, every source I opened for this problem names no AI system: the 2026 paper calls its work computer-assisted and names only non-AI tools, and the 1994, 2010, 2012 and 2019 works predate any relevant AI use. Searches for the problem with AI terms, and of AI-result trackers and news, found AI work on other problems (the dominating Hadwiger conjecture, the Erdős problems, the Jacobian and cycle double cover conjectures, a Hamiltonian-cycle problem) but nothing on this one. Several PDFs did not decode for me, zbMATH returned 403 and the Crossref lookup for the 1994 paper was rate-limited, so the 1994 statement and the Norin–Thomas theorem rest on secondary text, and the order-13 paper rests on a summarising read of its HTML version.
competing_reading: Read the order-13 result as a complete, settled restricted case. The authors say 'proving' in the abstract, the minimum-degree hypothesis covers all 6-connected order-13 graphs, and the large-graph theorem (plus the order-12 and order-13 cases) leaves only finitely many orders, each a finite set of graphs, below an unstated N; on that reading the problem has advanced. The opposing reading: each order is a finite set of graphs, so the order-13 result is an exhaustive check of one instance-size, which §2.1 says moves nothing about a universal claim; the large-graph theorem also leaves an unquantified range open; and the authors themselves say 'strengthens' in §1.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The full text of arXiv:2604.03433, from a PDF or TeX source, to see whether the order-13 argument is a structural proof with computer checks or a complete enumeration, and to confirm the exact theorem wording in §1 against §4. (2) The ancillary code (NewMMNA_code.pdf) and an independent rerun of the 13-vertex computations. (3) Peer review or publication of 2604.03433, or a later paper that cites it. (4) The 1994 Jørgensen paper, to confirm the conjecture's exact wording and the order-11 claim. (5) Whether a written Norin–Thomas theorem exists and what N_6 it gives, which would show whether the large-graph case has a second independent proof. (6) A numerical value of N in Kawarabayashi et al., which would fix the remaining range of sizes.

events.credibility_reason: Known only from talk abstracts and search snippets; no written proof located.

judgement.why: The statement is a universal claim over all 6-connected K6-minor-free graphs. The only post-snapshot event, the 2026 order-13 result, covers a single vertex count, which is a finite set of graphs, and the record says the argument is an exhaustive computer enumeration (nauty plus a minor search, 340 hours). That is a census of one finite instance-size, so I answered instances (F5) rather than case. The case reading turns on the large-N theorem leaving only finitely many orders. Even so, N is unstated and order 14 and above stay open, so the enumeration settles no infinite subclass. For consistency, the 2019 order-12 result is also instances. The large-graph, bounded-treewidth and girth-6 results restrict to infinite classes, so they are case results, each digested through JCTB or J. Combinatorics. The Norin–Thomas talk claim is a case result, unreviewed, and doubtful because no write-up exists. No AI system is named in any event; the 2026 paper's computer assistance is classical software.
judgement.doubts: The order-13 call between instances and case is close. If it were case, the problem would sit at partial with no AI involvement; the AI answer is none either way. The order-13 paper was read only through a summarising fetch of its HTML version.
judgement.by: judging pass (JUDGE.md), claude-opus-5-5; not the researching agent and not a human reviewer
